claim: The anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) plays a role in human memory formation, as evidenced by electrophysiological data.
source: Previously we reported electrophysiological evidence for a role for the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) in human memory formation (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).

claim: Theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the ATN predicted successful memory formation.
source: Theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) predicted successful memory formation, with the involvement of gamma oscillations suggesting memory-relevant local processing in the ATN.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014) mentioned in the abstract.

claim: Gamma oscillations suggest memory-relevant local processing in the ATN.
source: Theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) predicted successful memory formation, with the involvement of gamma oscillations suggesting memory-relevant local processing in the ATN.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the involvement of gamma oscillations in CFC.

claim: The importance of the theta frequency range in memory processing is well-established.
source: The importance of the theta frequency range in memory processing is well-established, and phase alignment of oscillations is considered to be necessary for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific consensus about theta oscillations and memory.

claim: Phase alignment of oscillations is considered to be necessary for synaptic plasticity.
source: The importance of the theta frequency range in memory processing is well-established, and phase alignment of oscillations is considered to be necessary for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about phase alignment and synaptic plasticity.

claim: Theta phase alignment in the ATN is necessary for memory encoding.
source: We hypothesized that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be necessary for memory encoding.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: Phase alignment in the theta rhythm was greater during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding.
source: Further analysis of the electrophysiological data reveal that phase alignment in the theta rhythm was greater during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding, and that this alignment was correlated with the CFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Theta phase alignment was correlated with theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling.
source: Further analysis of the electrophysiological data reveal that phase alignment in the theta rhythm was greater during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding, and that this alignment was correlated with the CFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis showing correlation between phase alignment and CFC.

claim: The findings support an active processing role for the ATN during memory formation.
source: These findings support an active processing role for the ATN during memory formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data on phase alignment and CFC.

claim: Animal and human lesion studies suggest that the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) may be involved as a part of an extended hippocampal-cortical encoding system.
source: Animal and human lesion studies suggest that the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) may also be involved as a part of an extended hippocampal-cortical encoding system (Harding et al., 2000; Vertes et al., 2001; van der Werf et al., 2003; Aggleton et al., 2010; Aggleton, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: The deep location and small size of the ATN has limited direct electrophysiological recording of the ATN during human memory formation.
source: However, the deep location and small size of the ATN has limited direct electrophysiological recording of the ATN during human memory formation (encoding).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the anatomical constraints of studying the ATN.

claim: Enhanced frontal cortex-right ATN (RATN) theta phase synchrony predicted successful memory encoding.
source: Enhanced frontal cortex-right ATN (RATN) theta phase synchrony and theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the RATN predicted successful memory encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).

claim: Theta-gamma CFC in the RATN predicted successful memory encoding.
source: Enhanced frontal cortex-right ATN (RATN) theta phase synchrony and theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the RATN predicted successful memory encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).

claim: RATN theta-gamma CFC during successful encoding suggested an active role for the RATN in memory formation.
source: Our initial findings of RATN theta-gamma CFC during successful encoding suggested an active role for the RATN in memory formation (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014), because gamma oscillations are believed to reflect local processing (Jensen et al., 2007), and the theta rhythm is well-known to be important in memory processing (Kahana et al., 2001; Hasselmo, 2002; Klimesch et al., 2004; Buzsáki, 2005; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Lega et al., 2012; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from CFC findings and citations to literature on gamma oscillations and theta rhythm.

claim: Gamma oscillations are believed to reflect local processing.
source: Our initial findings of RATN theta-gamma CFC during successful encoding suggested an active role for the RATN in memory formation (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014), because gamma oscillations are believed to reflect local processing (Jensen et al., 2007), and the theta rhythm is well-known to be important in memory processing (Kahana et al., 2001; Hasselmo, 2002; Klimesch et al., 2004; Buzsáki, 2005; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Lega et al., 2012; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2007.

claim: The theta rhythm is well-known to be important in memory processing.
source: Our initial findings of RATN theta-gamma CFC during successful encoding suggested an active role for the RATN in memory formation (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014), because gamma oscillations are believed to reflect local processing (Jensen et al., 2007), and the theta rhythm is well-known to be important in memory processing (Kahana et al., 2001; Hasselmo, 2002; Klimesch et al., 2004; Buzsáki, 2005; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Lega et al., 2012; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on theta rhythm and memory.

claim: An active role for the RATN in memory formation could involve learning-related processes within the RATN, reflected by RATN synaptic modification.
source: We hypothesized that an active role could involve learning-related processes within the RATN, reflected by RATN synaptic modification, and sought an electrophysiological marker of this process.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Synaptic modification only occurs when pre- and post-synaptic action potentials occur within a narrow time window.
source: Synaptic modification only occurs when pre- and post-synaptic action potentials occur within a narrow time window (Paulsen and Sejnowski, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Paulsen and Sejnowski, 2000.

claim: Phase alignment indicates an orderly temporal relationship between a stimulus and neural activity across successive stimulus epochs.
source: Phase alignment indicates an orderly temporal relationship between a stimulus and neural activity across successive stimulus epochs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about phase alignment.

claim: Oscillatory phase alignment is required for activity to fit within the narrow temporal window necessary for synaptic plasticity.
source: It has been suggested that oscillatory phase alignment—a re-setting of the phase in a particular frequency range within the neuronal population at the recording site with each new stimulus—is required for activity to fit within the narrow temporal window necessary for synaptic plasticity (Paulsen and Sejnowski, 2000; Rizzuto et al., 2003; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Düzel et al., 2005; Fell and Axmacher, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on phase alignment and synaptic plasticity.

claim: Long-term potentiation associated with long-term memory encoding occurs only during a particular phase of the theta oscillation.
source: More specifically, the long-term potentiation associated with long-term memory encoding has been shown in animal studies to occur only during a particular phase of the theta oscillation (Fell and Axmacher, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to animal studies (Fell and Axmacher, 2011).

claim: RATN theta (4–8 Hz) phase alignment was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding from 0.9–1.1 s poststimulus (T = 8.50, p = 0.00015; cluster-size permutation test: p = 0.048).
source: RATN theta (4–8 Hz) phase alignment was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding from 0.9–1.1 s poststimulus (two-sided T-test: T = 8.50, p = 0.00015; cluster-size permutation test: p = 0.048) (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and referenced figures.

claim: The difference in RATN theta phase alignment between successful and unsuccessful encoding was seen at an individual level in all 7 participants.
source: The difference was seen at an individual level in all 7 participants (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by individual participant data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: During successful encoding, the correlation between early frontal theta/alpha phase alignment and CFC was significant (r = 0.84, p = 0.019; FDR corrected p-value = 0.02).
source: During successful encoding, the correlation between early frontal theta/alpha phase alignment and CFC was significant (r = 0.84, p = 0.019; false discovery rate (FDR) corrected p-value = 0.02 with a maximum FDR level of q = 0.05, to account for the calculation of multiple correlations).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between early frontal theta/alpha phase alignment and CFC during unsuccessful encoding.
source: No significant correlation was observed during unsuccessful encoding, nor was there a correlation with early RATN or late frontal theta phase alignment during either successful or unsuccessful encoding (Figure 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing lack of correlation.

claim: There was no correlation between early RATN theta phase alignment and CFC during successful or unsuccessful encoding.
source: No significant correlation was observed during unsuccessful encoding, nor was there a correlation with early RATN or late frontal theta phase alignment during either successful or unsuccessful encoding (Figure 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing lack of correlation.

claim: There was no correlation between late frontal theta phase alignment and CFC during successful or unsuccessful encoding.
source: No significant correlation was observed during unsuccessful encoding, nor was there a correlation with early RATN or late frontal theta phase alignment during either successful or unsuccessful encoding (Figure 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing lack of correlation.

claim: The correlation between late RATN theta phase alignment and CFC was significant during successful encoding (r = 0.78, p = 0.039; FDR-adjusted p-value = 0.04 with q = 0.1).
source: The correlation was significant, however, between late RATN theta phase alignment and CFC applying the same frequency cut-offs (r = 0.78, p = 0.039). With a maximum FDR level of q = 0.1, the FDR-adjusted p-value was 0.04.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: Correlation between phase alignment and CFC was significantly greater during successful encoding compared to unsuccessful encoding.
source: These correlations were then directly compared between successful and unsuccessful encoding by calculating a z-score using the Fisher z-transform for each correlation coefficient and comparing the difference, corrected for sample size, to the unit normal distribution; correlation was significantly greater during successful encoding (criterion p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison using Fisher z-transform.

claim: A broadband (4–20 Hz) early poststimulus RATN phase alignment was identified.
source: Finally, we identified a broadband (4–20 Hz) early poststimulus RATN phase alignment, but unlike later RATN theta phase alignment, neither it nor the event-related potentials (ERPs) differed significantly between successful and unsuccessful encoding (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Early broadband RATN phase alignment did not differ significantly between successful and unsuccessful encoding.
source: Finally, we identified a broadband (4–20 Hz) early poststimulus RATN phase alignment, but unlike later RATN theta phase alignment, neither it nor the event-related potentials (ERPs) differed significantly between successful and unsuccessful encoding (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference.

claim: Event-related potentials (ERPs) did not differ significantly between successful and unsuccessful encoding.
source: Finally, we identified a broadband (4–20 Hz) early poststimulus RATN phase alignment, but unlike later RATN theta phase alignment, neither it nor the event-related potentials (ERPs) differed significantly between successful and unsuccessful encoding (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference.

claim: The ERP peak amplitude was correlated with the early RATN phase alignment during successful encoding (r = 0.75, p < 0.0001).
source: The ERP peak amplitude was correlated with the early RATN phase alignment during successful (r = 0.75, p < 0.0001) and during unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.70, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: The ERP peak amplitude was correlated with the early RATN phase alignment during unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.70, p < 0.0001).
source: The ERP peak amplitude was correlated with the early RATN phase alignment during successful (r = 0.75, p < 0.0001) and during unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.70, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between frontal ERP amplitude and frontal phase alignment.
source: There was no significant correlation between frontal ERP amplitude and frontal phase alignment (p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing lack of correlation.

claim: Frontal-RATN theta phase synchrony around 1 s post-stimulus during successful encoding correlated with frontal theta phase alignment (r = 0.88, p = 0.0098).
source: Frontal-RATN theta phase synchrony around 1 s post-stimulus during successful encoding correlated with frontal theta phase alignment (r = 0.88, p = 0.0098) at that time, but not with RATN phase alignment (p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: Frontal-RATN theta phase synchrony around 1 s post-stimulus during successful encoding did not correlate with RATN phase alignment.
source: Frontal-RATN theta phase synchrony around 1 s post-stimulus during successful encoding correlated with frontal theta phase alignment (r = 0.88, p = 0.0098) at that time, but not with RATN phase alignment (p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing lack of correlation.

claim: Frontal theta phase alignment correlated with the early phase synchrony episode across successful and unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.62, p = 0.019).
source: Both frontal and RATN theta phase alignment correlated with the early phase synchrony episode across successful and unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.62, p = 0.019 and r = 0.77, p = 0.0012, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: RATN theta phase alignment correlated with the early phase synchrony episode across successful and unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.77, p = 0.0012).
source: Both frontal and RATN theta phase alignment correlated with the early phase synchrony episode across successful and unsuccessful encoding (r = 0.62, p = 0.019 and r = 0.77, p = 0.0012, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: Frontal and RATN theta phase alignments were not significantly correlated with each other during either the early or the late time periods.
source: Frontal and RATN theta phase alignments were not significantly correlated with each other (p > 0.05) during either the early or the late time periods, consistent with their differing correlations with CFC and phase synchrony.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing lack of correlation.

claim: RATN theta phase alignment is likely to promote memory-related synaptic plasticity.
source: Theta phase alignment is likely to promote memory-related synaptic plasticity for two reasons. Firstly, phase alignment is deemed a pre-requisite for the synaptic plasticity underlying memory encoding, and secondly, the theta rhythm dominates in the hippocampus, a key structure involved in memory (Buzsáki, 2005; Fell et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2012), with animal studies indicating that hippocampal theta phase influences encoding success (Hasselmo, 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge and citations about phase alignment, theta rhythm, and memory.

claim: Phase alignment is deemed a pre-requisite for the synaptic plasticity underlying memory encoding.
source: Theta phase alignment is likely to promote memory-related synaptic plasticity for two reasons. Firstly, phase alignment is deemed a pre-requisite for the synaptic plasticity underlying memory encoding, and secondly, the theta rhythm dominates in the hippocampus, a key structure involved in memory (Buzsáki, 2005; Fell et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2012), with animal studies indicating that hippocampal theta phase influences encoding success (Hasselmo, 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about phase alignment and synaptic plasticity.

claim: The theta rhythm dominates in the hippocampus, a key structure involved in memory.
source: Theta phase alignment is likely to promote memory-related synaptic plasticity for two reasons. Firstly, phase alignment is deemed a pre-requisite for the synaptic plasticity underlying memory encoding, and secondly, the theta rhythm dominates in the hippocampus, a key structure involved in memory (Buzsáki, 2005; Fell et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2012), with animal studies indicating that hippocampal theta phase influences encoding success (Hasselmo, 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on hippocampal theta rhythm and memory.

claim: Animal studies indicate that hippocampal theta phase influences encoding success.
source: Theta phase alignment is likely to promote memory-related synaptic plasticity for two reasons. Firstly, phase alignment is deemed a pre-requisite for the synaptic plasticity underlying memory encoding, and secondly, the theta rhythm dominates in the hippocampus, a key structure involved in memory (Buzsáki, 2005; Fell et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2012), with animal studies indicating that hippocampal theta phase influences encoding success (Hasselmo, 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to animal studies (Hasselmo, 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).

claim: Greater RATN theta phase alignment during successful than unsuccessful memory formation, and its correlation with CFC during successful encoding, is compatible with the suggestion that memory-related changes occur within the RATN itself.
source: We interpret our findings of greater RATN theta phase alignment during successful than unsuccessful memory formation, and its correlation with CFC during successful encoding, as compatible with the suggestion that memory-related changes occur within the RATN itself.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data on phase alignment and CFC.

claim: The phase alignment in the theta rhythm provides the timing necessary for local synaptic modification and is further reflected in gamma oscillations, thought to reflect local information processing.
source: The phase alignment in the theta rhythm provides the timing necessary for local synaptic modification and is further reflected in gamma oscillations, thought to reflect local information processing (Jensen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and citation to literature on gamma oscillations.

claim: RATN phase alignment could be produced as a downstream consequence of hippocampal phase alignment, and need not derive from independent local RATN processing.
source: It should be noted that RATN phase alignment could be produced as a downstream consequence of hippocampal phase alignment, and need not derive from independent local RATN processing.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative alternative interpretation.

claim: The fact that phase alignment occurs in the RATN is suggestive of RATN-specific synaptic modifications.
source: Irrespective of its origin, however, the fact that phase alignment occurs in the RATN is suggestive of RATN-specific synaptic modifications.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation of phase alignment in the RATN.

claim: Integration of head direction and movement information in the ATN in rats suggests an active processing role for the ATN theta rhythm.
source: Our interpretation is supported by the finding that integration of head direction and movement information in the ATN in rats suggests an active processing role for the ATN theta rhythm (Tsanov et al., 2013), and that hippocampal theta oscillations appear to modulate theta-related plasticity in the ATN (Tsanov et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to animal studies (Tsanov et al., 2013).

claim: Hippocampal theta oscillations appear to modulate theta-related plasticity in the ATN.
source: Our interpretation is supported by the finding that integration of head direction and movement information in the ATN in rats suggests an active processing role for the ATN theta rhythm (Tsanov et al., 2013), and that hippocampal theta oscillations appear to modulate theta-related plasticity in the ATN (Tsanov et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to animal studies (Tsanov et al., 2011).

claim: Early post-stimulus frontal theta/alpha phase alignment predicted subsequent CFC.
source: Early post-stimulus frontal theta/alpha phase alignment also predicted subsequent CFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the correlation data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Early phase synchrony reflects enhanced item-specific attention and perceptual processing of the stimulus.
source: We interpreted the early phase synchrony as reflecting enhanced item-specific attention and perceptual processing of the stimulus (Düzel et al., 2005; Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014) and attention allocation has been found to oscillate at a theta rhythm (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Attention allocation has been found to oscillate at a theta rhythm.
source: We interpreted the early phase synchrony as reflecting enhanced item-specific attention and perceptual processing of the stimulus (Düzel et al., 2005; Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014) and attention allocation has been found to oscillate at a theta rhythm (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fiebelkorn et al., 2013.

claim: The correlation between early frontal theta phase alignment and later CFC fits with the necessity of early processing for successful memory formation.
source: The correlation between the accompanying early frontal theta phase alignment and later CFC fits with the necessity of this early processing for successful memory formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correlation data.

claim: The broadband early RATN phase alignment resembled rhinal cortex and hippocampus findings with similar timing reported during both successful retrieval and correct rejection of new items.
source: The broadband early RATN phase alignment we identified resembled rhinal cortex and hippocampus findings with similar timing reported during both successful retrieval and correct rejection of new items (Mormann et al., 2005), interpreted as an unspecific memory processing facilitator.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mormann et al., 2005.

claim: Broadband phase alignment in rhinal cortex and hippocampus has been interpreted as an unspecific memory processing facilitator.
source: The broadband early RATN phase alignment we identified resembled rhinal cortex and hippocampus findings with similar timing reported during both successful retrieval and correct rejection of new items (Mormann et al., 2005), interpreted as an unspecific memory processing facilitator.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mormann et al., 2005.

claim: The correlation between the early RATN phase alignment and the RATN ERP is consistent with the suggestion that broadband phase re-setting is reflected in the ERP.
source: The correlation between the early RATN phase alignment and the RATN ERP is consistent with the suggestion that broadband phase re-setting is reflected in the ERP (Mormann et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citation to Mormann et al., 2005.

claim: The early RATN phase alignment likely reflects the N1 component of the visual evoked response, which is related to memory performance.
source: Indeed the early RATN phase alignment likely reflects the N1 component of the visual evoked response, which is related to memory performance (Klimesch et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citation to Klimesch et al., 2004.

claim: The similarity between the phase alignment in the RATN and that detected in the rhinal cortex and hippocampus suggests the early phase alignment was a memory-task-related phenomenon.
source: The similarity between the phase alignment identified here in the RATN and that detected in the rhinal cortex and hippocampus suggests the early phase alignment observed here was also a memory-task-related phenomenon, which is plausible given that a preceding practice session meant our task involved intentional encoding (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the similarity to prior findings.

claim: The finding provides further support for the hypothesis that the RATN is a part of an extended hippocampal system supporting memory encoding.
source: Our finding provides further support for the hypothesis that the RATN is a part of an extended hippocampal system supporting memory encoding (Aggleton et al., 2010; Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Diverse neural correlates of memory formation have been reported around 1 s post-stimulus.
source: Diverse neural correlates of memory formation have been reported around 1 s post-stimulus (Paller et al., 1987; Schott et al., 2002; Sederberg et al., 2003; Osipova et al., 2006; Lega et al., 2012; Hanslmayr and Staudigl, 2014; Long et al., 2014), suggesting convergence of different processes underpinning encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on memory formation.

claim: Diverse neural correlates around 1 s post-stimulus suggest convergence of different processes underpinning encoding.
source: Diverse neural correlates of memory formation have been reported around 1 s post-stimulus (Paller et al., 1987; Schott et al., 2002; Sederberg et al., 2003; Osipova et al., 2006; Lega et al., 2012; Hanslmayr and Staudigl, 2014; Long et al., 2014), suggesting convergence of different processes underpinning encoding.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cited literature.

claim: RATN theta oscillations are involved in two separate processes: modulation of frontal-RATN theta oscillations through long-range synchrony and modulation of RATN gamma oscillations through CFC.
source: We postulate that RATN theta oscillations are involved in two separate processes: modulation of frontal-RATN theta oscillations through long-range synchrony and modulation of RATN gamma oscillations through CFC.
evidence: The claim is a postulated interpretation of the data.

claim: The RATN has an integrative role, in accord with the diverse inputs received by this nucleus.
source: This suggests an integrative role for the RATN, in accord with the diverse inputs received by this nucleus.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the postulated dual role of RATN theta oscillations.

claim: Granger causality calculation was consistent with frontal activity driving the theta phase synchrony with RATN activity.
source: Granger causality calculation was consistent with frontal activity driving the theta phase synchrony with RATN activity (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior analysis (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).

claim: The correlation between frontal theta phase alignment and frontal-RATN theta phase synchrony occurred because frontal theta phase alignment facilitates the phase synchrony.
source: We postulate that the correlation between frontal theta phase alignment, which was independent of encoding success, and frontal-RATN theta phase synchrony occurred because frontal theta phase alignment facilitates the phase synchrony.
evidence: The claim is a postulated interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: The narrow time window indicated by early frontal theta phase alignment is consistent with an early, rapid perceptual response.
source: The narrow time window indicated by early frontal theta phase alignment is consistent with an early, rapid perceptual response, and the correlation with the phase synchrony suggests both measures reflect the same process.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the timing of the phase alignment.

claim: The correlation between early frontal theta phase alignment and phase synchrony suggests both measures reflect the same process.
source: The narrow time window indicated by early frontal theta phase alignment is consistent with an early, rapid perceptual response, and the correlation with the phase synchrony suggests both measures reflect the same process.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correlation data.

claim: The correlation between early frontal theta phase alignment and later intra-RATN CFC is consistent with the requirement of early stimulus processing for successful later memory formation processes.
source: The correlation between early frontal theta phase alignment and later intra-RATN CFC is consistent with the requirement of early stimulus processing for successful later memory formation processes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correlation data.

claim: Frontal and RATN phase alignments reflect different contributions to memory formation.
source: We interpret the frontal and RATN phase alignments, which were not correlated with each other, as reflecting different contributions to memory formation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the lack of correlation between frontal and RATN phase alignments.

claim: Frontal phase alignment was correlated with phase synchrony, whereas the RATN phase alignment was correlated with CFC, supporting the interpretation that they reflect different contributions to memory formation.
source: This interpretation is further supported by the finding that frontal phase alignment was correlated with phase synchrony, whereas the RATN phase alignment was correlated with CFC.
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by the differential correlation patterns.

claim: Alignment of RATN theta oscillatory phase during successful memory encoding provides the temporal precision necessary for synaptic plasticity.
source: Alignment of RATN theta oscillatory phase during successful memory encoding provides the temporal precision necessary for synaptic plasticity and correlates with the theta-gamma CFC taking place as a memory is established.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data on phase alignment and its correlation with CFC.

claim: Intrathalamic signals were recorded from the ATN and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei bilaterally from 7 human volunteers undergoing electrode placement for subsequent stimulation treatment of pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy.
source: Intrathalamic signals from the ATN and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei bilaterally and neocortical activity from simultaneous surface EEG were recorded from 7 human volunteers undergoing electrode placement for subsequent stimulation treatment of pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and participants.

claim: Neocortical activity from simultaneous surface EEG was recorded from 7 human volunteers.
source: Intrathalamic signals from the ATN and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei bilaterally and neocortical activity from simultaneous surface EEG were recorded from 7 human volunteers undergoing electrode placement for subsequent stimulation treatment of pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Frontal electrodes were located at Fz (frontal), AFz (anterior frontal), or Fpz (frontopolar).
source: Frontal electrodes, whose placement was limited by surgical dressing location, were located at Fz (frontal), AFz (anterior frontal), or Fpz (frontopolar).
evidence: The claim describes the electrode placement in the experimental methods.

claim: The reported data were taken from the most frontal available electrode from each participant.
source: The reported data were taken from the most frontal available electrode from each participant as previously reported (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the data selection method.

claim: The electrophysiological data were recorded during presentation of a series of photographic scenes, which were judged as indoors or outdoors.
source: The electrophysiological data were recorded during presentation of a series of photographic scenes, which were judged as indoors or outdoors.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental task.

claim: Each scene was labeled as successfully or unsuccessfully encoded on the basis of a subsequent recognition test.
source: Each scene was labeled as successfully or unsuccessfully encoded on the basis of a subsequent recognition test, in which the scenes were presented again, mixed with new scenes, and judged as 'old' or 'new'.
evidence: The claim describes the method for classifying encoding success.

claim: The thalamic data were re-referenced offline by subtracting the deeper neighbor rendering a bipolar reference.
source: The thalamic data were re-referenced offline by subtracting the deeper neighbor rendering a bipolar reference.
evidence: The claim describes the data preprocessing method.

claim: Phase alignment was obtained by calculating the phase-locking factor, which is a stimulus-locked average of phase distribution across trials at a given time-frequency.
source: Phase alignment was obtained by calculating the phase-locking factor, which is a stimulus-locked average of phase distribution across trials at a given time-frequency (Tallon-baudry et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim describes the method for calculating phase alignment, supported by citation.

claim: The phase alignment index (0 = no phase alignment; 1 = complete phase alignment) was obtained by dividing the length of the unit phase vector across epochs for each participant by the number of epochs.
source: The phase alignment index (0 = no phase alignment; 1 = complete phase alignment), was obtained by dividing the length of the unit phase vector across epochs for each participant by the number of epochs (Düzel et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim describes the method for calculating the phase alignment index, supported by citation.

claim: Numbers of trials were balanced for successful and unsuccessful encoding.
source: Numbers of trials were balanced for successful and unsuccessful encoding.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design to control for trial number effects.

claim: Two-sided T-tests were used to compare phase alignment during successful vs unsuccessful encoding.
